overview.title: Testing the instruction-tuned Gemma: better answers, same hallucinations
overview.main_topic: Qualitative evaluation of the LoRA instruction-fine-tuned Gemma 1B: it now answers questions, but still hallucinates.
overview.central_idea: After one epoch of LoRA instruction tuning, Gemma responds to instructions in the trained format and stops with [end], instead of continuing the prompt; yet it still confidently invents an answer to an impossible question, which instruction tuning can only partly mitigate (e.g., by training refusals).
overview.importance: It shows concretely what supervised instruction tuning buys (format and helpfulness) and what it does not (factual grounding), motivating RLHF and the later discussion of hallucination.
learning_objectives: Prompt a fine-tuned model using the exact training template.
Describe the behavioural change instruction tuning produced.
Explain why instruction tuning does not fix hallucination.
Describe how training on refusal responses can reduce some hallucinations.
prerequisites: The base model's hallucination on the same question (p.511)

summary:
Having fine-tuned Gemma 1B with LoRA on the Dolly instructions (listing 16.14, p.517), the authors check whether it now follows directions. They call `gemma_lm.generate()` with prompts written in the **exact training template**, `"[instruction]\n…[end]\n[response]\n"`, and `max_length=512`.

Asked *How can I make brownies?*, the model replies with a recipe-like answer: mix flour, sugar, butter, milk and chocolate chips, bake in a 9x13 pan for 30 minutes at 350°F, optionally add vanilla, and it ends with `[end]`. Asked *What is a proper noun?*, it gives a reasonable definition with examples ("The White House", "The Eiffel Tower"), again terminated by `[end]`. The authors' verdict: **"Much better."** The model now **responds to questions instead of simply carrying on the thought of the prompt text**, which was the problem with the base model on p.510-511.

*Note (not in the book):* the answers are fluent but not flawless: the recipe lists "1/2 cup of chocolate chips" twice and omits eggs, a small reminder that fluency is not correctness.

Then the key test: **Have we solved the hallucination problem?** Asked *Who is the 542nd president of the United States?*, the model answers confidently, "The 542nd president of the United States was James A. Garfield." The answer: **"Not at all."** Instruction tuning can still make **some inroads**: a common technique is to train on many instruction/response pairs whose desired response is a refusal such as `"I don't know"` or `"As a language model, I cannot help you with that"`, teaching the model to avoid answering topics where it would often give poor-quality results.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Asks whether fine-tuning improved instruction following and tries it.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The evaluation here is qualitative: a few hand-picked prompts, formatted with the training template.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The 55% next-token accuracy from p.517 does not tell you whether the model behaves like an assistant; sample outputs do.

paragraphs.excerpt: Much better. Our model will now respond to questions, instead of trying to
paragraphs.what_it_says: The outputs are much better: the model now responds to questions rather than continuing the prompt text.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Before tuning, Gemma treated a question as the beginning of some web document and continued it (p.510-511). After tuning, the most likely continuation of `[response]\n` is an answer that ends with `[end]`.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the behavioural change that makes a base LM usable as a chatbot, achieved with only ~1.3M trainable parameters (p.517).
paragraphs.technical_idea: The `[end]` marker learned from RESPONSE_TEMPLATE lets the generation be cut off cleanly; without it the model would keep producing text up to max_length.

terminology.meaning: Producing a response that does what the prompt asks, rather than merely continuing it.

connections: p.511: base Gemma behaved like a 'fancy autocomplete for the internet'.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Hallucination is not solved, but instruction tuning can help by training on many pairs whose desired response is a refusal like "I don't know", so the model avoids topics where it would give poor answers.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The model has no built-in notion of 'I don't know'; it outputs the most probable continuation. Garfield was a real president (the 20th), so the model blends plausible fragments. Supervised examples of refusals make declining a probable continuation for certain kinds of questions.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets realistic expectations: data can shape when a model declines, but does not give it reliable knowledge of its own ignorance. This leads to RLHF (p.519) and to the 'whack-a-mole' discussion on p.522.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Refusal training is the same supervised fine-tuning as before; only the targets change.

A trained answer declining to respond, e.g. 'I don't know'.

concepts.name: Instruction fine-tuning
concepts.definition: Further training of a pretrained LLM on instruction/response pairs with the next-token loss.
concepts.intuition: Teach the autocomplete that the natural continuation of a question is an answer.
concepts.technical: Here done with LoRA rank 8 on Dolly for one epoch; prompts must use the training template.
concepts.significance: Turns continuation behaviour into answering behaviour.
concepts.example: Brownie and proper-noun answers on this page.
concepts.misconception: That it removes hallucinations; the 542nd-president answer shows it does not.

concepts.name: Hallucination
concepts.definition: Fluent, confident output that is factually wrong or unsupported.
concepts.intuition: A student who always writes something plausible rather than leaving a blank.
concepts.technical: Follows from maximizing likelihood of continuations without a mechanism to verify facts or express uncertainty.
concepts.significance: Called a fundamental problem of language models (p.512).
concepts.example: 'The 542nd president of the United States was James A. Garfield.'
concepts.misconception: That better instruction following implies better factuality.

concepts.name: Refusal training
concepts.definition: Including instruction/response pairs whose target response is a refusal or 'I don't know'.
concepts.intuition: Showing the student examples where the right answer is to say 'I'm not sure'.
concepts.technical: Ordinary supervised fine-tuning with refusal strings as targets for selected prompts.
concepts.significance: Makes some inroads against hallucination on specific topics.
concepts.example: "As a language model, I cannot help you with that".
concepts.misconception: That it teaches true self-knowledge; it teaches which kinds of prompts to decline.

code.title: Prompting the fine-tuned model with the training template
code.original_code:
>>> gemma_lm.generate(
...     "[instruction]\nHow can I make brownies?[end]\n"
...     "[response]\n",
...     max_length=512,
... )
[instruction]
How can I make brownies?[end]
[response]
You can make brownies by mixing together 1 cup of flour, 1 cup of sugar, 1/2
cup of butter, 1/2 cup of milk, 1/2 cup of chocolate chips, and 1/2 cup of
chocolate chips. Then, you can bake it in a 9x13 pan for 30 minutes at 350
degrees Fahrenheit. You can also add a little bit of vanilla extract to the
batter to make it taste better.[end]
>>> gemma_lm.generate(
...     "[instruction]\nWhat is a proper noun?[end]\n"
...     "[response]\n",
...     max_length=512,
... )
[instruction]
What is a proper noun?[end]
[response]
A proper noun is a word that refers to a specific person, place, or thing.
Proper nouns are usually capitalized and are used to identify specific
individuals, places, or things. Proper nouns are often used in formal writing
and are often used in titles, such as "The White House" or "The Eiffel Tower."
Proper nouns are also used in titles of books, movies, and other works of
literature.[end]
code.what_it_does: Generates responses to two instructions formatted exactly like the training prompts.

line_explanations.explanation:
Python concatenates the two adjacent string literals into `[instruction]
How can I make brownies?[end]
[response]
`, matching PROMPT_TEMPLATE; `max_length=512` caps prompt + output tokens.
Output includes the prompt followed by the generated recipe, ending with the learned `[end]` marker.
Same pattern for 'What is a proper noun?'; a coherent definition ending with `[end]`.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: a templated prompt string. Output: prompt + generated response as one string.
code.algorithm: Autoregressive decoding with the model's default sampler until an end condition or max_length.
code.theory_link: Generating only after the `[response]` marker, as described on p.513.

parameters.name: max_length
parameters.role: Maximum total sequence length in tokens.

pitfalls: Prompts must match the training template; different markers would make the fine-tuning much less effective.
Whether generation stops at `[end]` depends on stop-token configuration; here the model simply produced it and nothing further was printed.

code.title: Testing hallucination with an impossible question
code.original_code:
>>> gemma_lm.generate(
...     "[instruction]\nWho is the 542nd president of the United States?[end]\n"
...     "[response]\n",
...     max_length=512,
... )
[instruction]
Who is the 542nd president of the United States?[end]
[response]
The 542nd president of the United States was James A. Garfield.[end]
code.what_it_does: Asks about the 542nd US president; the model confidently answers 'James A. Garfield'.

line_explanations.explanation: A fluent, false answer ending with `[end]`.

code.theory_link: Likelihood maximization does not imply truthfulness.
pitfalls: Outputs vary with sampling and weights; you may get a different wrong name.

deeper.title: Why Garfield?
deeper.body: The question pattern 'Who is the Nth president of the United States?' is overwhelmingly followed by a president's name in training text. The model has learned the format of such answers, not a check that N ≤ the number of presidents. It produces a high-probability name from that pattern; the same answer appeared from the base model on p.511, suggesting fine-tuning changed format, not knowledge.

deeper.title: What changed and what didn't
deeper.body: Changed: the model's response style (answers instead of continuations), its use of `[end]`, and its tone. Unchanged: its factual knowledge and calibration, which come from pretraining. This matches p.512's description of fine-tuning as nudging tone and content rather than learning a new latent space.

deeper.title: Confident guesser analogy
deeper.body: A quiz contestant trained only to buzz in and answer will answer even a nonsense question. Training them on examples where the correct move is to say 'pass' helps for familiar kinds of trick questions, but does not give them a reliable sense of which questions they truly cannot answer.

misconceptions.correction: The page shows the fine-tuned model still invents a 542nd president; the authors answer 'Not at all.'
Even the brownie recipe repeats an ingredient and omits eggs (observation not in the book).

misconceptions.claim: Any prompt format works after fine-tuning.
misconceptions.correction: The book prompts with the exact training template, which the model has learned to answer.

misconceptions.claim: Refusal training makes the model know what it does not know.
misconceptions.correction: It trains the model to avoid specific topics where it often gives poor answers; the authors claim only 'some inroads'.

takeaways:
Prompts at inference use the exact training template `[instruction]
…[end]
[response]
`.
After LoRA instruction tuning, Gemma answers questions and ends with `[end]` instead of continuing the prompt.
Hallucination is not solved: the model still names a '542nd president'.
Training on refusal responses ('I don't know') can reduce hallucinations on specific topics.
Fine-tuning shapes format and behaviour more than factual knowledge.

options: The model responds to questions instead of continuing the prompt text
questions.answer: The model responds to questions instead of continuing the prompt text

questions.question: Why does each prompt on this page include `[instruction]` and `[response]` markers?
questions.answer: Because the model was fine-tuned on that template; matching it triggers the learned answering behaviour after `[response]`.

questions.question: Why doesn't supervised instruction tuning on Dolly fix hallucinations?
questions.answer: It teaches response format and style, but the model still outputs the most probable continuation without any mechanism to verify facts or recognize impossible questions.
questions.explanation: The page shows the confident Garfield answer; p.512 calls hallucination fundamental.

questions.answer: The model learned RESPONSE_TEMPLATE's stop marker and emits it when its answer is complete.
